title: Dissecting and Modeling the Architecture of Modern GPU Cores
problem: Academic GPU microarchitecture simulators such as Accel-sim rely on pipeline models derived from NVIDIA Tesla (2006), missing 15+ years of GPU core evolution including compiler-guided dependency management, the L0 instruction cache, register file cache, and updated issue logic in Ampere-class SMs. This causes simulation inaccuracy that misleads research conclusions.
method: The authors reverse-engineer the NVIDIA Ampere (RTX A6000) SM pipeline using hand-written SASS microbenchmarks that measure cycle-precise instruction timings. They uncover a software-hardware co-design dependency mechanism using per-warp Stall counters and six Dependence counters (SBx) encoded as ISA control bits replacing traditional scoreboards, a Compiler-Guided Greedy-Then-Youngest (CGGTY) warp issue policy, a two-bank register file without collector units, a compiler-managed 6-entry register file cache (RFC), an L0 instruction cache with a 16-entry stream buffer prefetcher, and detailed memory pipeline queue sizing and latencies. All findings are integrated into a rebuilt Accel-sim model validated against real hardware.

title: EXION: Exploiting Inter-and Intra-Iteration Output Sparsity for Diffusion Models
problem: Diffusion model inference requires up to 1000 denoising iterations through transformer blocks (dominant 38-100% of operations), resulting in excessive energy consumption and latency; existing transformer accelerators target only QKV projection and attention computation within a single iteration and do not exploit the iterative structure or the dominant FFN layer overhead.
method: EXION is a SW-HW co-designed diffusion accelerator exploiting two types of output sparsity. First, the FFN-Reuse algorithm identifies temporal data redundancy across iterations in FFN GELU outputs: one dense iteration is computed fully, then N sparse iterations reuse the GELU output for low-magnitude elements (achieving 70-97% sparsity in the 1st FFN layer, reducing FFN ops by 52-85%). Second, an improved eager prediction algorithm using two-step leading-one detection (TS-LOD) predicts attention scores via log-domain approximation to identify and skip negligible attention computation within each iteration (20-95% intra-iteration sparsity, skipping avg. 26% Q and 22% KV projections). The ConMerge data compaction mechanism converts resulting unstructured sparse output matrices into compact dense forms via column condensing (removing all-zero columns) and block merging (merging sparse and dense tiled blocks using conflict-vector tracking). The dedicated hardware Diffusion-Sparsity Aware Core (DSC) contains: a Sparse-Dense Unified Engine (SDUE) with a 16x16 DPU array with per-DPU input/weight/conflict-vector switches enabling flexible ConMerge-aware dataflow; a ConMerge Assistant Unit (CAU) with sparsity-level sorting and ConMerge vector generation; an Eager Prediction Engine (EPRE) with TS-LOD-enhanced log-domain DPU array; and a Configurable SIMD Engine (CFSE) for special functions. Synthesized at 14nm, 800MHz, 0.8V.

title: Scaling Deep Learning Training with MPMD Pipeline Parallelism
problem: GSPMD/SPMD-based pipeline parallelism in JAX can only encode GPipe-style schedules; it cannot express MPMD schedules like 1F1B or Interleaved 1F1B that improve memory efficiency and throughput, and it forces homogeneous stages with poor scalability over low-bandwidth (DCN) inter-node links.
method: JaxPP extends JAX with a MPMD pipeline parallelism runtime. Users annotate model code with pipeline_yield calls that mark stage boundaries; JaxPP infers stages from data dependencies. An accumulate_grads API implements the gradient accumulation loop with user-specified schedules (1F1B, Interleaved 1F1B). A single-controller driver process traces the JAX computation to a task graph, assigns tasks to SPMD actors (each actor manages one or more devices with a local SPMD mesh), and infers send/receive pairs using topological ordering to avoid deadlocks. Buffer deletion is handled by a liveness pass. All task dispatches are fused into a single RPC per actor. A loop commuting pass handles weight sharing (tied embeddings) efficiently.

title: LAVA: Lifetime-Aware VM Allocation with Learned Distributions and Adaptation to Mispredictions
problem: VM scheduling in hyperscale cloud data centers is NP-hard with incomplete lifetime information; one-shot lifetime predictions accumulate mispredictions over time, causing host fragmentation and wasted capacity.
method: LAVA: three lifetime-aware algorithms using distribution-based VM lifetime prediction. ML model: GBDT trained on VM features (zone, family, shape, SSD, project metadata) to predict E(Tr|Tu) — conditional expected remaining lifetime given observed uptime. Multiple training examples per VM by augmenting with Tu quantiles. Model compiled into Borg scheduler binary (<10us latency, 780x faster than LA-Binary's inference server). Three algorithms: (1) NILAS — non-invasive reprediction tie-breaker using max repredicted exit time of co-scheduled VMs; (2) LAVA — lifetime-class based host state machine (open/recycling) placing shorter-lived VMs in gaps of longer-lived hosts, upgrading/downgrading host lifetime class on mispredictions; (3) LARS — lifetime-guided migration ordering for defragmentation, migrating longest-lived VMs first to let shorter VMs exit naturally.

title: LightNobel: Improving Sequence Length Limitation in Protein Structure Prediction Model via Adaptive Activation Quantization
problem: Protein Structure Prediction Models (PPMs) such as AlphaFold2 and ESMFold use a Pair Representation tensor with dimension (Ns, Ns, Hz) that grows quadratically in memory and cubically in attention score computation with sequence length Ns, causing GPU out-of-memory failures beyond ~2000 amino acids and latency dominated (>91%) by Triangular Attention at long sequences. Existing chunking and low-memory attention workarounds do not reduce the fundamental activation size and degrade performance.
method: LightNobel applies Token-wise Adaptive Activation Quantization (AAQ) that exploits a distogram pattern unique to PPM: activations in the Pair Representation have large inter-token variance but small inter-channel variance, making token-wise quantization preferable to channel-wise. AAQ classifies Pair Representation activations into three groups based on value range and outlier density, applying INT8 inliers + INT16 outliers (Group A, high-magnitude pre-LayerNorm), INT4 inliers + INT16 outliers (Group B, post-LayerNorm with some outliers), and INT4 inliers without outlier handling (Group C, low-magnitude). Outliers are identified at runtime using a dynamic top-k algorithm on the VVPU via bitonic sorting. The hardware implements a Reconfigurable Matrix Processing Unit (RMPU) with bit-level reconfigurable adder trees and Reconfigurable Data Aligners (RDAs) that partition tokens into 4-bit chunks and dynamically configure PE Lanes (4 or 5 PE Lanes) to handle multi-precision token streams without per-element dequantization. A Versatile Vector Processing Unit (VVPU) with 128 SIMD Lanes and a Local Crossbar Network handles LayerNorm, Softmax, residual connections, and runtime quantization. A token-wise MHA dataflow similar to FlashAttention avoids materializing the full (Ns, Ns, Ns) score matrix. The design is synthesized at 28nm targeting 1 GHz with 5 HBM2E stacks (80 GB).
